info.desc: Modern Life Is Rubbish is the second album by English alternative rock band Blur, released in May 1993. The album peaked at number 15 on the UK Album Chart and featured the singles "For Tomorrow, "Chemical World" and "Sunday Sunday". The earlier single "Popscene" was added to the American release of the album. Although their debut album Leisure (1991) had been commercially successful, Blur faced a severe media backlash soon after its release, and fell out of public favour. podcast.body: This album was a turning point for Blur and the Britpop movement. Following EMI's investment in Food Records, Blur gained significantly more resources, promotion, and development, including more interesting music videos. Some publications consider it the first official album of the Britpop movement, or at least it contained two key elements that would define the Britpop sound by 1995: Graham Coxon's guitars and Damon Albarn's lyrics, which were rich in British content and exalted the United Kingdom. The album's promotion also heavily featured classic British iconography like the Union Jack, Doc Martens, and Fred Perry polos. Critically, it was much better received than "Leisure," sounding fresh and distinct from the Manchester movement, though not yet considered a masterpiece.
